pharm: Enhances the inhibitory action of GABA at the GABA-A receptor, increasing chloride conductance to produce sedation, anxiolysis, amnesia, anticonvulsant and muscle-relaxant effects
quick: IV sedation: 0.5-2 mg titrated slowly; individualise (lower in elderly/with opioids)
Not applicable for injection; oral syrup may be given without regard to food
Avoid near term (neonatal sedation/withdrawal); use only if essential
Small amounts in milk; brief interruption may be advised after dosing
Active metabolite accumulates in renal failure - reduce dose, prolonged effect
Reduced clearance - lower dose, titrate carefully
Avoid - additive CNS and respiratory depression
Respiration, oxygen saturation, BP and heart rate continuously
summary: Midazolam is a short-acting benzodiazepine used for procedural and pre-operative sedation, anxiolysis and amnesia, induction of general anaesthesia, sedation of ventilated patients, and (oral/buccal/intranasal forms) treatment of seizures including status epilepticus. It is given IV, IM, orally, buccally or intranasally and must be titrated slowly to effect. It carries a BOXED WARNING: IV midazolam can cause profound respiratory depression and arrest, especially outside critical-care settings, and concomitant use with opioids can cause profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma and death. It is HABIT FORMING (a controlled benzodiazepine) and use must be limited and monitored. Reserve only for settings with continuous respiratory/cardiac monitoring and resuscitation facilities; flumazenil is the reversal agent.
indications: Pre-operative sedation, anxiolysis and amnesia (IM or IV)
Conscious/procedural sedation before or during diagnostic, therapeutic or endoscopic procedures (IV)
Continuous sedation of intubated and mechanically ventilated patients (IV infusion)
Treatment of acute seizures / status epilepticus (buccal, intranasal or IM/IV depending on product)

dosage.d: Initial small increments e.g. 0.5-2 mg IV over at least 2 minutes, titrated to effect; usual total often <=5 mg
dosage.t: Titrate slowly; wait 2+ minutes between increments
dosage.n: Reduce by >=30% if opioids/other CNS depressants are co-administered

dosage.d: 0.07-0.08 mg/kg IM about 1 hour before surgery (commonly ~5 mg)
Reduce dose (e.g. initial IV increments <=1-1.5 mg) and titrate slowly
dosage.n: Increased sensitivity and risk of apnoea

dosage.r: Acute prolonged or repetitive seizures / status epilepticus
dosage.d: Age/weight-banded buccal or intranasal dose per product (e.g. buccal 2.5-10 mg by age band)
dosage.t: Single dose; repeat per protocol if needed

admin: Use only in settings with continuous monitoring of respiratory and cardiac function (e.g. pulse oximetry) and immediate availability of resuscitation drugs and equipment
Give IV slowly in small increments, allowing at least 2 minutes to assess effect before redosing
Have flumazenil and ventilation/intubation equipment immediately available
Reduce the dose substantially when used with opioids or other CNS depressants and in the elderly, debilitated or hepatically/renally impaired
Do not give rapid IV bolus (risk of apnoea and hypotension)
Some injectable products contain benzyl alcohol - avoid in neonates
moa: Midazolam binds to the benzodiazepine site of the GABA-A receptor complex and potentiates the effect of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA, increasing the frequency of chloride channel opening. This hyperpolarises neurons and depresses CNS activity, producing dose-dependent sedation, anxiolysis, anterograde amnesia, anticonvulsant and centrally mediated muscle-relaxant effects. Its water-soluble formulation becomes lipophilic at physiologic pH, giving rapid CNS penetration and a short onset and duration.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to midazolam or other benzodiazepines
Intrathecal or epidural administration (formulations may contain preservatives/benzyl alcohol)
relative: Severe respiratory insufficiency / acute respiratory depression
Concomitant opioids or other CNS depressants (profound sedation/respiratory depression)
Myasthenia gravis, severe hepatic impairment, shock or congestive cardiac failure
Sleep apnoea; elderly and debilitated patients
History of alcohol or substance use disorder (dependence/abuse risk)
monitor: Respiratory rate and oxygen saturation continuously
Signs of dependence/withdrawal with prolonged use

preg: Benzodiazepines cross the placenta. Use late in pregnancy or during labour can cause neonatal sedation, hypotonia, respiratory depression and withdrawal (floppy-infant syndrome). Avoid unless essential; if used, monitor the neonate.
lact: Midazolam and its metabolite pass into breast milk in small amounts. After a single dose for a procedure, breastfeeding can usually resume once the mother is alert; with repeated dosing monitor the infant for sedation and poor feeding.
renal: The active metabolite alpha-hydroxymidazolam (and its glucuronide) accumulates in renal failure, causing prolonged and deepened sedation, especially with infusions. Reduce the dose, extend dosing intervals and monitor closely.
hepatic: Hepatic impairment reduces clearance and prolongs the half-life of midazolam. Reduce the dose and titrate carefully; sedation may be deeper and longer.

major: Opioids and other CNS depressants - profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma and death (boxed warning); reduce doses and monitor
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g. ketoconazole, itraconazole, clarithromycin, ritonavir, grapefruit) - markedly increase midazolam levels and effect
Strong CYP3A4 inducers (e.g. rifampicin, carbamazepine, St John's wort) - reduce efficacy
moderate: Other sedatives, antipsychotics, sedating antihistamines, antidepressants - additive CNS depression
minor: Moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g. fluconazole, erythromycin, diltiazem) - increased exposure
interactions.food: Grapefruit juice inhibits CYP3A4 and increases oral midazolam levels - avoid
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - additive CNS and respiratory depression
interactions.diagnostics: No specific laboratory interference; monitor clinically

common: Pain or reaction at the injection site
serious: Respiratory depression and apnoea, especially with rapid IV injection or with opioids
Dependence and withdrawal with prolonged use

monitoring: Continuous respiratory monitoring (rate and pulse oximetry)
Depth of sedation and airway patency throughout and after the procedure
Recovery before discharge (ensure return of psychomotor function)
Signs of dependence, tolerance or withdrawal with prolonged infusion
counsel: This medicine causes drowsiness and memory loss - you may not remember the procedure
Do not drive, operate machinery, sign legal documents or drink alcohol for at least 24 hours after sedation
Have a responsible adult accompany you home and stay with you
Tell staff about all other medicines, especially opioids, sleeping tablets or alcohol use
Midazolam can be habit forming - take it only as prescribed and do not stop a long course abruptly
Avoid grapefruit juice with oral midazolam
pk: IV onset within 1-5 minutes; IM 15 minutes; oral/buccal/intranasal within ~10-15 minutes
IV peak effect within minutes; IM Tmax ~30 minutes
Elimination half-life approximately 1.5-3 hours (prolonged in elderly, hepatic/renal impairment and obesity)
Sedation lasts roughly 1-2 hours after a single dose; longer with infusions or impaired clearance
Store injection at controlled room temperature, protect from light; do not freeze; check product for benzyl alcohol content
pearls: BOXED WARNING: IV midazolam can cause fatal respiratory depression/arrest; opioid co-use can cause coma and death
Habit forming - a controlled benzodiazepine; limit use and taper after prolonged infusions
Titrate slowly in small increments and wait >=2 minutes between doses; reduce with opioids and in the elderly
Flumazenil reverses sedation but is short-acting - watch for re-sedation
Active metabolite accumulates in renal failure (prolonged sedation); reduce dose in hepatic/renal impairment
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (incl. grapefruit) markedly raise levels; only use with full monitoring and resuscitation backup
missed: Midazolam is given by clinicians for procedures, anaesthesia or seizures rather than on a routine home schedule, so there is usually no missed dose. For seizure-rescue products, follow the action plan provided and do not repeat sooner than instructed.
overdose: Overdose causes exaggerated CNS and respiratory depression: drowsiness, confusion, ataxia, hypotension, respiratory depression, coma and apnoea, which can be fatal, especially with other CNS depressants. Provide airway support and ventilation, monitor vital signs, and use flumazenil as a specific antagonist (with caution in benzodiazepine-dependent patients or mixed overdoses due to seizure and re-sedation risk).
